title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Accomplishments
Here are the variables we will explore.

took.ACT
ACTCompositeScore
ap.exam
cte.achievement
total.cte.courses.taken
MCA.M
MCA.R
MCA.S

HIGH SCHOOL ACCOMPLISHMENT VARIABLES AND HIGHEST CREDENTIAL LEVEL (Among credential completers only, n=48,162)
The accomplishment variables show the strongest and most consistent associations with credential level of any variable group, and the academic achievement versus CTE engagement divide is at its sharpest here.
took.ACT shows a very strong association with credential level (φ=0.332). ACT takers complete bachelor’s or higher credentials at 74.5% compared to just 30.4% for non-takers — a gap of 44.1 percentage points. Non-takers hold sub-baccalaureate credentials at 69.6% versus 25.5% for ACT takers. Among all categorical accomplishment variables, ACT participation is the single strongest predictor of whether a completer reaches the baccalaureate level.
ap.exam shows an even stronger association (φ=0.292). AP exam takers complete bachelor’s or higher at 87.1% — the highest rate of any categorical predictor examined — compared to 58.4% for non-takers. Only 12.9% of AP exam takers stop at the sub-baccalaureate level. AP participation is the clearest high school signal that a graduate will pursue and complete a four-year credential.
ACT Composite Score shows the largest continuous variable gap (F=6632.2). Bachelor’s or higher completers score 3.98 composite points above sub-baccalaureate completers — a very large difference on a 36-point scale. This is the strongest single continuous variable association in the entire postsecondary analysis.
MCA Math (F=4166.8), MCA Reading (F=5113.5), and MCA Science (F=3871.3) all show large and consistent gaps. Sub-baccalaureate completers score approximately 0.56 standard deviations below bachelor’s or higher completers on Math, 0.48 below on Reading, and 0.52 below on Science. The consistency across all three assessments reinforces the finding that academic achievement is a powerful and pervasive predictor of credential level among completers.
cte.achievement shows a strong association in the opposite direction (V=0.213). CTE concentrators and completors hold sub-baccalaureate credentials at 43.7% — more than double the rate for No CTE graduates (20.0%) and well above CTE participants (30.7%). The gradient is monotonic and steep. No CTE graduates complete bachelor’s or higher at 80.0% compared to just 56.3% for CTE concentrators. The association between CTE concentration and sub-baccalaureate credential completion is the strongest inverse relationship in the accomplishment group and directly mirrors the positive association with regional employment seen throughout the analysis.
Total CTE courses taken shows a large and highly significant association (F=3780.6). Sub-baccalaureate completers take on average 1.84 more CTE courses than bachelor’s or higher completers — nearly two full courses more. This is the largest continuous variable mean difference for any accomplishment variable predicting credential level and confirms the dose-response nature of the CTE engagement and sub-baccalaureate credential relationship.
The accomplishment findings for credential level complete the chain of evidence established across the postsecondary analysis. High academic achievement in high school — ACT participation, AP exam participation, high MCA scores — strongly and consistently predicts bachelor’s or higher credential attainment. CTE engagement — particularly at the concentrator level and measured as total courses taken — strongly and consistently predicts sub-baccalaureate credential attainment. These two sorting mechanisms operate in opposite directions and are essentially the same mechanisms that sort graduates into out-of-region versus regional employment outcomes a decade later.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Demographics
Here are the variables we will be exploring;

Gender
economic.status
RaceEthnicity
SpecialEdStatus

DEMOGRAPHIC VARIABLES AND POSTSECONDARY PATHWAY (Among credential completers only, n=47,959)
The ps.pathway variable combines credential level and graduation location into six categories: sub-baccalaureate region (19.2%), bachelor or higher region (21.3%), sub-baccalaureate MN (7.6%), bachelor or higher MN (21.5%), sub-baccalaureate outside MN (4.8%), and bachelor or higher outside MN (25.5%). This is the most analytically complete postsecondary outcome variable and the one that most directly maps onto the three workforce pathway framework.
Gender shows a moderate association with ps.pathway (V=0.086). The most notable differences are in sub-baccalaureate regional completion — males complete at 20.9% compared to 17.9% for females — and bachelor or higher regional completion — females at 23.1% compared to 19.1% for males. Females show modestly higher bachelor or higher MN completion (22.4% vs. 20.3%). The out-of-state pathways are essentially equivalent across genders (bachelor or higher outside MN: 26.0% female vs. 24.9% male). The gender difference is primarily in the regional pathways — males are more concentrated in sub-baccalaureate regional completion while females are more concentrated in bachelor or higher regional completion — rather than in geographic mobility.
Economic status shows a strong association with ps.pathway (V=0.191). Low-income graduates are dramatically more concentrated in sub-baccalaureate regional completion (32.0% vs. 16.4%) and sub-baccalaureate MN completion (10.9% vs. 6.9%), while non-low-income graduates dominate bachelor or higher outside MN completion (28.1% vs. 13.8%) and bachelor or higher MN completion (22.6% vs. 16.6%). Bachelor or higher regional completion is essentially equal across economic status groups (21.5% vs. 20.6%). The economic gradient is concentrated in credential level and out-of-state geographic mobility — low-income completers are channeled toward sub-baccalaureate regional and MN pathways, while non-low-income completers access four-year and out-of-state pathways at substantially higher rates.
Special education status shows a strong association with ps.pathway (V=0.175). Special education completers are concentrated in sub-baccalaureate regional completion (42.7% vs. 18.1%) and sub-baccalaureate MN completion (17.6% vs. 7.2%), while showing very low rates of bachelor or higher MN (7.0% vs. 22.2%) and bachelor or higher outside MN (11.9% vs. 26.1%) completion. The pattern is the most extreme of any demographic variable — among special education graduates who complete credentials, over 60% do so through sub-baccalaureate pathways, and the majority of those complete regionally.
Race and ethnicity shows a moderate association (V=0.097) with substantial within-group variation. The Unknown category again shows an anomalous pattern — 57.2% sub-baccalaureate regional and 23.5% sub-baccalaureate MN — consistent with a non-traditional student population concentrated in community and technical colleges. Among identified groups, Hispanic graduates show the highest sub-baccalaureate regional rate (38.5%) followed by Black (29.0%) and American Indian (22.2%) graduates, all substantially above White (17.7%) and Asian/PI (17.1%) graduates. Bachelor or higher outside MN is highest for Asian/PI (27.5%) and White (26.5%) graduates, with substantially lower rates for Black (15.7%), Hispanic (15.9%), and American Indian (16.0%) graduates. American Indian graduates show the highest bachelor or higher MN rate (32.1%), followed by Asian/PI (30.2%), consistent with in-state four-year credential completion being a relatively common pathway for these groups among those who reach the baccalaureate level.
The ps.pathway findings synthesize the patterns seen across the individual postsecondary dependent variables. Economic disadvantage and special education status concentrate graduates in sub-baccalaureate regional pathways — the credential completion route most directly associated with regional workforce attachment in Stage 3. Non-low-income and non-special-education graduates access four-year and out-of-state pathways at substantially higher rates, which the Stage 3 findings show are associated with out-of-region employment and geographic departure from Minnesota. Gender differences are modest and concentrated in the regional pathways rather than geographic mobility. Racial and ethnic minority graduates — particularly Hispanic and Black — show elevated sub-baccalaureate regional completion rates that, combined with the Stage 3 workforce findings, suggest these graduates are more likely to achieve regional workforce attachment through the college completer pathway than their White and Asian/PI peers.

data <- master.original %>%
  filter(!highest.cred.level %in% c("Did not graduate ps", "Attending ps"),
         ps.grad.location != "Did not graduate ps") %>%
  mutate(highest.cred.level = as_factor(highest.cred.level),
         ps.grad.location = as_factor(ps.grad.location),
         ps.pathway = case_when(
    
    # Never attended or attended but did not graduate
    highest.cred.level == "Did not graduate ps" & 
      ps.grad.location == "Did not grad" ~ "Did not graduate ps",
    highest.cred.level == "No college"         ~ "Did not graduate ps",
    
    # Sub-baccalaureate by location
    highest.cred.level == "Less than Bachelors" & 
      ps.grad.location == "PS grad region"      ~ "Sub-baccalaureate - region",
    highest.cred.level == "Less than Bachelors" & 
      ps.grad.location == "PS grad MN"          ~ "Sub-baccalaureate - MN",
    highest.cred.level == "Less than Bachelors" & 
      ps.grad.location == "PS grad outside MN"  ~ "Sub-baccalaureate - outside MN",
    
    # Bachelor or higher by location
    highest.cred.level == "Bachelors or higher" & 
      ps.grad.location == "PS grad region"      ~ "Bachelor or higher - region",
    highest.cred.level == "Bachelors or higher" & 
      ps.grad.location == "PS grad MN"          ~ "Bachelor or higher - MN",
    highest.cred.level == "Bachelors or higher" & 
      ps.grad.location == "PS grad outside MN"  ~ "Bachelor or higher - outside MN",
    
    # Currently attending - treat as its own category
    ps.grad.location == "Attending ps"          ~ "Attending ps",

text:
High School Characteristics
Here are the variables we will be exploring;

Dem_Desc
avg.unemp.rate

HIGH SCHOOL CHARACTERISTICS AND POSTSECONDARY PATHWAY (Among credential completers only, n=47,959)
EDR shows a meaningful association with ps.pathway (V=0.125). The most striking difference is in sub-baccalaureate MN completion — EDR 9 graduates complete at 11.6% compared to just 6.0% for EDR 10 graduates, nearly double the rate. EDR 10 graduates show substantially higher bachelor or higher outside MN completion (27.9% vs. 19.8%), consistent with the geographic mobility pattern identified in earlier analyses. Bachelor or higher regional completion is modestly higher for EDR 9 (24.3% vs. 20.1%), while sub-baccalaureate regional completion is similar across EDRs (19.5% vs. 18.4%). Bachelor or higher MN completion is essentially identical (21.6% vs. 21.3%). The EDR pattern clarifies the mechanism underlying the Stage 3 workforce outcome differences — EDR 9 graduates who complete credentials are more likely to do so at sub-baccalaureate and baccalaureate levels within Minnesota, producing stronger in-state out-of-region employment, while EDR 10 graduates are more likely to complete credentials outside Minnesota and leave the state entirely.
Average local unemployment rate shows a statistically significant association with ps.pathway (F=49.1) with a clear ordering. Sub-baccalaureate regional graduates come from communities with the lowest average unemployment of any pathway group. All other pathways show significantly higher unemployment rates, with sub-baccalaureate MN (difference=0.315), sub-baccalaureate outside MN (difference=0.291), and bachelor or higher region (difference=0.227) all substantially above the regional sub-baccalaureate group. Sub-baccalaureate MN and sub-baccalaureate outside MN are not significantly different from each other (difference=-0.024, p=0.987). Bachelor or higher outside MN (difference=0.095) is significantly above sub-baccalaureate regional but below all other sub-baccalaureate pathways.
This is a counterintuitive finding worth careful interpretation. Graduates who complete sub-baccalaureate credentials regionally come from the strongest local labor markets — not the weakest. This suggests that regional sub-baccalaureate completion is not primarily driven by economic necessity or lack of alternatives, but rather by a genuine regional orientation that coexists with relatively strong local employment conditions. Graduates from higher-unemployment communities are more likely to pursue credentials outside the region — either at in-state institutions in stronger labor markets or out of state entirely — consistent with weaker local conditions pushing credential-seeking graduates toward more geographically distant opportunities.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Accomplishments
Here are the variables we will explore.

took.ACT
ACTCompositeScore
ap.exam
cte.achievement
total.cte.courses.taken
MCA.M
MCA.R
MCA.S

HIGH SCHOOL ACCOMPLISHMENT VARIABLES AND POSTSECONDARY PATHWAY (Among credential completers only, n=47,959)
The accomplishment variables show their strongest and most differentiated associations with ps.pathway, which as the most complete postsecondary outcome variable reveals the full sorting mechanism operating from high school through credential completion.
took.ACT is the strongest categorical predictor of ps.pathway (V=0.333). Non-ACT takers are concentrated in sub-baccalaureate regional (40.3%) and sub-baccalaureate MN (19.3%) completion, with very low bachelor or higher MN (8.4%) and bachelor or higher outside MN (10.8%) rates. ACT takers show the opposite profile — dominated by bachelor or higher outside MN (27.9%), bachelor or higher MN (23.7%), and bachelor or higher regional (23.0%), with low sub-baccalaureate regional (15.7%) and very low sub-baccalaureate MN (5.7%) rates. ACT participation is functioning as a near-perfect sorter between sub-baccalaureate and baccalaureate credential pathways across all geographic locations.
ap.exam shows the second strongest association (V=0.322). AP exam takers are heavily concentrated in bachelor or higher outside MN (36.6%) and bachelor or higher MN (30.6%), with very low sub-baccalaureate regional (8.5%) and sub-baccalaureate MN (2.5%) rates. Non-AP takers show the reverse — sub-baccalaureate regional (24.8%) is their largest single pathway category, and bachelor or higher outside MN (19.8%) is their second largest. AP participation is the strongest predictor of the bachelor or higher MN pathway specifically (30.6% vs. 16.8%) — a finding with direct workforce implications given that bachelor or higher MN graduates show the highest meaningful MN employment rates at Years 5 and 10 in Stage 3.
ACT Composite Score shows very large mean differences across pathways (F=1777.0). The ordering is clear and consistent: bachelor or higher outside MN and bachelor or higher MN score highest and are not significantly different from each other (difference=0.038, p=0.986). Bachelor or higher regional scores approximately 2.32 points below both. Sub-baccalaureate regional scores the lowest among single-state pathways, and sub-baccalaureate MN and sub-baccalaureate outside MN score approximately 0.45 and 0.26 points below sub-baccalaureate regional respectively — though sub-baccalaureate outside MN is not significantly different from sub-baccalaureate regional (p=0.240). The convergence of bachelor or higher MN and bachelor or higher outside MN at nearly identical ACT scores is analytically important — geographic destination after completing a four-year credential is not primarily driven by academic achievement but by other factors.
MCA Math (F=968.4), MCA Reading (F=1087.8), and MCA Science (F=937.3) all show the same two-cluster structure at the pathway level. The bachelor or higher MN and bachelor or higher outside MN pathways are not significantly different from each other on any of the three assessments (Math p=0.439, Reading p=0.992, Science p=1.000). Sub-baccalaureate regional and sub-baccalaureate outside MN are not significantly different on Math (p=0.572) or Science (p=0.800), and only marginally different on Reading (p=0.791). This two-cluster structure — sub-baccalaureate pathways at lower scores, bachelor or higher pathways at higher scores — is the clearest expression of credential level as the primary sorting mechanism, with geographic location playing a secondary role within each credential level cluster.
cte.achievement shows a strong association with ps.pathway (V=0.162). CTE concentrators are most concentrated in sub-baccalaureate regional (25.4%) completion — more than double the rate for No CTE graduates (12.3%) — and show the lowest bachelor or higher outside MN rate (20.1%) of any CTE category. No CTE graduates dominate bachelor or higher outside MN (31.9%) and bachelor or higher MN (27.5%). Bachelor or higher regional completion is essentially flat across CTE categories (20.4%, 23.2%, 20.6%), confirming that CTE engagement does not meaningfully influence whether a bachelor’s graduate stays in the region — it operates primarily through the credential level and sub-baccalaureate regional sorting mechanism. The sub-baccalaureate outside MN and sub-baccalaureate MN gaps between concentrators and No CTE graduates (6.8% vs. 3.1% and 11.3% vs. 4.6%) suggest that even among sub-baccalaureate completers, CTE engagement is associated with more geographically proximate credential completion.
Total CTE courses taken (F=834.9) confirms the dose-response pattern throughout. Sub-baccalaureate regional graduates take the most CTE courses, significantly above all other pathways. Sub-baccalaureate MN and sub-baccalaureate outside MN graduates also take substantially more courses than bachelor or higher graduates of any geographic type. Bachelor or higher MN and bachelor or higher outside MN graduates are not significantly different from each other (difference=0.161, p=0.001 — marginally significant but very small in practical terms), again confirming that geographic destination within the four-year pathway is not meaningfully driven by CTE engagement.
The ps.pathway accomplishment findings are the most analytically complete picture of how high school experiences sort graduates into postsecondary pathways. The primary sorting mechanism is credential level — academic achievement predicts four-year completion while CTE engagement predicts sub-baccalaureate completion — and this sorting operates across all geographic destinations. The secondary sorting mechanism within credential level is geographic — for sub-baccalaureate completers, CTE engagement predicts regional completion; for four-year completers, academic achievement above the already-high threshold does not further differentiate geographic destination. These two mechanisms together produce the workforce pathway structure identified throughout the analysis.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
This research examined which factors most strongly influence whether individuals achieve meaningful employment within Southern Minnesota’s region (EDR 9 & 10) after high school. Using both contingency table analysis (effect sizes, trends over 1, 5, and 10 years) and CART modeling, the goal was to identify which variables most reliably anchor individuals in the regional workforce versus those that push them toward statewide mobility, disconnection, or outmigration.
A special focus was also placed on non-college graduates, who represent a substantial share of the region’s young adults and are at higher risk of disconnection from the labor force. Understanding their pathways provides additional insights into how to build a stronger, more inclusive regional workforce.
The findings provide a roadmap for education and workforce policy, showing how demographics, high school context, accomplishments, and postsecondary experiences interact to shape local labor market attachment.

Using both contingency table analysis (effect sizes, trends over 1, 5, and 10 years) and CART modeling, the goal was to identify which variables most reliably anchor individuals in the regional workforce versus those that push them toward statewide mobility, disconnection, or outmigration.
A special focus was also placed on non-college graduates, who represent a substantial share of the region’s young adults and are at higher risk of disconnection from the labor force. The findings provide a roadmap for education and workforce policy, showing how demographics, high school context, accomplishments, and postsecondary experiences interact to shape local labor market attachment.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Relationships - Employment

Total Summary
Across demographics, high school characteristics, accomplishments, and postsecondary experiences, clear themes emerge about what most strongly predicts meaningful employment in the region versus disconnection or statewide mobility.

Postsecondary experiences are the strongest predictors overall. Where a student graduates from, whether they graduate, and what credential they earn all have lasting effects on both regional retention and statewide opportunities.
Economic status and special education needs stand out among demographics as powerful predictors of early disadvantage and disconnection.
On the other hand, career and technical education (CTE) consistently boosts regional employment, making it a strong anchor to the local workforce.
Meanwhile, academic rigor variables (ACT, AP, MCA scores) largely point students toward postsecondary enrollment and careers beyond the region, signaling statewide mobility rather than regional attachment. Finally, some variables — particularly language indicators and one-off tests like SAT — show weak or inconsistent predictive value.




1. Strong Predictors of Regional Employment and Disconnection
These variables consistently show strong or moderate effect sizes and clear differences in meaningful regional employment, making them strong candidates for modeling.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




ps.grad.location
Postsecondary
Strongest predictor of regional employment. Local PS grads most likely to stay; out-of-region grads more mobile/disconnected.


ps.grad
Postsecondary
Graduation itself reduces disconnection and improves both regional and statewide employment.


highest.cred.level
Postsecondary
Sub-baccalaureate grads anchor regionally; higher credentials = statewide mobility.


ps.grad.InstitutionSector
Postsecondary
Public 2-year grads most tied to regional workforce; 4-year grads more mobile.


economic.status
Demographic
Low-income students more disconnected and less likely to be regionally employed, especially early.


SpecialEdStatus
Demographic
Special education students face large, persistent disadvantages in regional employment.


Dem_Desc
HS Characteristic
Rural grads more likely to stay regionally; metro grads more mobile and more disconnected.


CTE achievement
Accomplishment
Concentrators/completors consistently most likely to work regionally.


total.cte.courses.taken
Accomplishment (cont.)
More CTE courses = stronger regional employment attachment.






2. Moderate Predictors — Some Association, Less Consistency
These variables show moderate associations with outcomes. They may be useful in modeling, particularly when combined with other predictors.








Variable
Type
Key Insights




RaceEthnicity
Demographic
Persistent disparities: Black, AI, and Hispanic students more disconnected; Asian students more PS-enrolled/out-of-region.


Gender
Demographic
Early gap: males more regionally employed, females more PS-attending. Gaps narrow over time.


Grad.year.covid
Demographic
Post-COVID grads slightly more disconnected and more likely in local work early on.


ACTCompositeScore
Accomplishment (cont.)

MCA Math, Reading, Science
Accomplishment (cont.)
Higher scores = statewide employment and PS; lower scores = regional work.


avg.unemp.rate
HS Characteristic (cont.)
Higher unemployment counties = more disconnection, weaker early outcomes.


avg.wage.pct.state

Higher local wages = lower disconnection, somewhat stronger employment.






3. Weak or Inconsistent Predictors — Candidates for Dropping
These variables showed very weak associations and could be considered for dropping from modeling, unless interaction effects suggest added value.

Accomplishment

Overall Conclusion
The most consistent predictors of regional workforce retention are sub-baccalaureate postsecondary pathways, public 2-year institutions, and CTE engagement, combined with rural high school origins. Meanwhile, academic rigor variables and 4-year degrees drive statewide mobility rather than regional employment. Disadvantage markers such as low-income status and special education needs are persistent risk factors for disconnection.
In short, the analysis reveals a dual pipeline:

CTE and 2-year credentials anchor students to Southern Minnesota’s workforce.
High academic achievement and 4-year+ credentials lead to mobility and employment beyond the region.

This suggests that interventions to strengthen the regional workforce should prioritize CTE pathways, 2-year institutions, and supports for low-income and special education students, while also recognizing that academic high-achievers are more likely to leave the region.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Relationships - Post-secondary
Across all four postsecondary outcomes — attended.ps, ps.grad, ps.grad.InstitutionSector, ps.grad.location, and highest.cred.level — consistent patterns emerge about which factors shape educational attainment and how these pathways tie into regional workforce retention versus mobility and disconnection.
The evidence is clear: postsecondary experiences are the strongest predictors of long-term employment outcomes, but they are deeply influenced by demographic background, high school context, and student accomplishments. This creates a dual-pipeline system: one that anchors students to Southern MN through CTE and sub-baccalaureate credentials, and another that channels academically strong students into statewide or national mobility through 4-year and higher pathways.


1. Attending Postsecondary Education

Key Predictors: Economic status (low-income less likely to attend), race/ethnicity (persistent gaps), and special education status (lower attendance).

Takeaway: Disadvantaged students are disproportionately less likely to enroll in PS at all, putting them at high risk of long-term disconnection.




2. Postsecondary Graduation (ps.grad)

Key Predictors: Economic status and SPED remain barriers to completion; racial gaps persist; academic readiness improves odds of graduating.

Takeaway: Simply completing PS dramatically reduces disconnection and boosts employment. Non-completers remain the most vulnerable group in the workforce pipeline.




3. Institution Sector of Graduation (ps.grad.InstitutionSector)

Key Predictors:

Academic rigor and PSEO → 4-year completions.

CTE engagement, SPED, and low-income → 2-year completions.


Takeaway: Institution type sorts students into applied versus academic pathways. Since 2-year completions are more strongly tied to regional employment, CTE and disadvantage groups inadvertently form the backbone of Southern MN’s workforce, while academically strong students pursue more mobile 4-year pathways.




4. Location of Graduation (ps.grad.location)

Key Predictors:

Disadvantaged students (low-income, SPED, marginalized race/ethnicity) → more likely to graduate in Southern MN.

High scorers and PSEO participants → more likely to graduate outside the region (other MN or out-of-state).

Local economic conditions (lower wages, higher unemployment) → stronger Southern MN completions.


Takeaway: Regional completions are most common among disadvantaged groups and CTE students, reinforcing their role in regional workforce stability.




5. Highest Credential Earned (highest.cred.level)

Key Predictors:

Academic rigor (ACT, MCA) and PSEO → bachelor’s or higher.

CTE engagement, low-income, SPED, disadvantaged counties → associate or sub-associate.


Takeaway: Credential level is the clearest stratifier of opportunity. Bachelor’s+ aligns with mobility, while associate/sub-associate aligns with regional employment.




Overall Conclusion
The postsecondary pipeline is shaped by two reinforcing forces:

Mobility Pipeline:

Driven by academic rigor and PSEO.
Leads to 4-year+ degrees, completions outside the region, and statewide mobility.
Most common among advantaged, higher-scoring students.

Regional Pipeline:

Driven by CTE engagement, 2-year institutions, economic disadvantage, SPED, and lower-wage/unemployment counties.
Leads to associate/sub-associate degrees and Southern MN completions, strongly tied to meaningful regional employment.
Most common among disadvantaged students who remain anchored locally.


In short: Southern MN’s workforce stability relies heavily on the regional pipeline of 2-year and CTE-driven pathways, which disproportionately serve low-income and SPED students. Meanwhile, academically strong and advantaged students pursue 4-year and higher credentials, fueling statewide and out-of-state mobility.
Policy Implication: To strengthen the regional workforce, interventions should both (1) support disadvantaged students in completing and leveraging their 2-year pathways and (2) create incentives for academically strong students to remain engaged in the region after completing higher degrees.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Prediction - Employment CART

Main takeaway
Across all three binary comparisons and all time horizons (1, 5, and 10 years after graduation), the CART models consistently highlight a dual pipeline shaping workforce outcomes in Southern Minnesota:

Anchors to Regional Employment:

CTE engagement and depth (≥2–5 courses, concentrator/completor status).
Sub-baccalaureate pathways (2-year credentials, certificates, some college).
Regional postsecondary attendance and graduation.
Favorable local economic conditions (competitive wages, lower unemployment).

Pathways to Statewide Mobility or Disconnection:

Bachelor’s degree attainment and high academic achievement (ACT ≥25–28, MCA Reading ≥4) consistently predict outward mobility into statewide labor markets.
Weak academic readiness (low ACT, low MCA scores) and lack of CTE engagement predict disconnection (no record, not attending PS).
Structural disadvantages (low-income, SpecialEd status, some racial/ethnic groups) persistently raise the risk of disconnection across all timeframes.


The synthesis underscores that CTE and regional postsecondary pathways are the backbone of workforce retention, while higher academic achievement and 4-year credentials lead to broader mobility. Disadvantaged groups remain at elevated risk of disconnection without targeted supports.



Year 1 after Graduation

Anchors: Early anchoring comes primarily from CTE engagement, math proficiency, and local labor market strength.
Barriers: SpecialEd involvement, weak academic readiness, and lack of CTE drive early disconnection or statewide mobility.
Interpretation: At this stage, exposure to CTE and basic academic preparation are critical to prevent graduates from being disconnected from work or education.




Year 5 after Graduation

Anchors: Regional postsecondary engagement, CTE depth, and sub-baccalaureate completion are most decisive.
Barriers: 4-year/Bachelor’s attainment predicts mobility out of the region; SpecialEd, gender, and racial disparities continue to shape risks of disconnection.
Interpretation: Mid-career, institutional pathways (regional PS, CTE credentials) dominate as anchors, while higher academic achievement channels students outward.




Year 10 after Graduation

Anchors: Long-term anchoring depends on regional postsecondary graduation, sustained CTE involvement, and competitive wage environments.
Barriers: Weak academic scores, lack of PS/CTE ties, and subgroup inequities push graduates toward disconnection or employment outside the region.
Interpretation: At this stage, outcomes stabilize: CTE and regional PS pipelines anchor students, while 4-year pathways and weak local wages reinforce outward movement or disconnection.




Overall Summary
The CART analyses converge on three central insights:

CTE engagement is the most consistent predictor of regional employment. Even minimal exposure is protective, while concentrator/completor status provides the strongest anchor.
Regional postsecondary pathways matter profoundly. Attendance and completion in Southern Minnesota institutions substantially increase the odds of regional employment at 5 and 10 years.
Mobility vs. disconnection split.

Mobility: High achievers and 4-year graduates are more likely to find meaningful employment statewide.
Disconnection: Students with weak academic readiness, limited CTE, and structural disadvantages face higher risks of no employment record or PS engagement.


This duality reflects a regional workforce pipeline rooted in CTE and 2-year credentials, contrasted with a mobility pipeline driven by academic achievement and 4-year degrees.



Policy/Practice Implications

Expand and deepen CTE opportunities, ensuring more students complete concentrator/completor pathways and take multiple courses (≥2–5).
Strengthen regional postsecondary connections, positioning 2-year institutions as central anchors for workforce retention.
Elevate sub-baccalaureate pathways as critical contributors to regional workforce strength.
Design retention strategies for 4-year graduates and high academic achievers, offering internships, research, and professional opportunities tied to local industries.
Target supports for vulnerable groups (low-income, SpecialEd, racial/ethnic subgroups) to reduce disconnection.
Maintain competitive local wages and employment opportunities to counter outward mobility and anchor graduates long-term.

In short, the models reaffirm that Southern Minnesota’s workforce is sustained by CTE and 2-year credentials, but retaining academically strong and 4-year graduates will require intentional strategies. Meanwhile, addressing equity gaps and economic competitiveness is essential to prevent long-term disconnection.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Prediction - post-secondary

Overall Model Performance
Across both dependent variables — postsecondary graduation location and highest credential earned — the pre-pruned CART models achieved accuracies of 61.7% and 64.2%, respectively. Both represented clear improvements over baseline distributions and showed that a relatively small set of predictors consistently explains meaningful variation in student pathways.
While not capturing all individual-level complexity, these models highlight distinct sets of academic, demographic, and experiential variables that shape whether students remain anchored in the Southern MN workforce pipeline or pursue mobility pathways.


Key Predictors Across Models
The following predictors emerged as the most consistently influential:

Academic readiness: MCA Reading and ACT Composite Score.
Economic status: Persistent disadvantages for low-income students.
Race/Ethnicity: White and Asian/PI students more likely to reach higher credentials; Black, AI, and Hispanic students more often concentrated in lower or incomplete outcomes.
PSEO participation: Steers students toward bachelor’s+ and out-of-region completions.
CTE engagement (courses taken): Reinforces regional and sub-baccalaureate pathways.

These predictors operate in two clear pipelines — one driving local attachment through sub-baccalaureate credentials, and one fostering mobility through advanced credentials.


Interpretation of Pathways

1. Graduation Location (ps.grad.location)

Regional completions clustered among economically disadvantaged students with moderate academic readiness.
Non-completion was strongly tied to low ACT and MCA scores, often regardless of background.
High academic readiness and PSEO participation predicted completions outside the region, fueling mobility pathways.

Implication: Regional institutions disproportionately serve disadvantaged students who achieve moderate readiness, while high scorers leave the region for completion.


2. Highest Credential Earned (highest.cred.level)

Bachelor’s or higher credentials were most strongly linked to high MCA and ACT scores, advantaged status, and PSEO participation.
Non-completion was almost guaranteed for students with low MCA Reading or ACT scores, even when other factors were favorable.
Associate or lower credentials (though less prominent in the tree structure) align with CTE-heavy pathways, serving as stabilizers for the regional workforce.

Implication: Academic readiness acts as the primary gateway to bachelor’s+ attainment, but economic and racial inequities remain barriers, even among high scorers.



Synthesis of Findings
Together, the models reinforce the existence of a dual-pipeline system in Southern Minnesota:

Regional Workforce Pipeline

Driven by CTE engagement, associate-or-lower credentials, and regional completions.
Anchors students with economic disadvantage and moderate readiness into the local labor market.
Provides workforce stability but limits long-term mobility and earning potential.

Mobility Pipeline

Driven by academic rigor, bachelor’s+ attainment, PSEO participation, and out-of-region completions.
Attracts advantaged, high-scoring students, who are least likely to remain in the region after completion.
Fuels statewide and out-of-state labor markets more than the local workforce.




Policy Implications

Strengthen regional anchors: Expand academic and financial supports for disadvantaged, moderate scorers to ensure successful completions in Southern MN institutions.
Address inequities in bachelor’s+ attainment: Target resources for high-achieving but low-income and underrepresented students to reduce barriers to advanced credentials.
Leverage CTE strategically: Maintain CTE as a stabilizer but ensure stackable pathways to prevent students from being locked into sub-associate outcomes.
Engage high-achievers locally: Create incentives and career opportunities that connect PSEO participants and bachelor’s+ completers back to the region to mitigate brain drain.



Conclusion
The predictive analysis confirms that academic readiness, economic status, and experiential factors like PSEO and CTE are the primary levers shaping postsecondary pathways. These pathways, in turn, determine whether students are most likely to remain in the Southern MN workforce or pursue mobility.
Ultimately, the models illustrate a structural duality: disadvantaged students with modest preparation form the backbone of the regional workforce through 2-year and regional completions, while advantaged high scorers are systematically funneled into statewide mobility. Policy efforts must therefore balance supporting the regional anchor pipeline with developing mechanisms to retain or re-engage mobile students after higher attainment.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Relationships - non-college grads
For non-college graduates, the central question is whether they secure meaningful employment in their home region. The evidence shows that regional employment is influenced most strongly by students’ accomplishments during high school, with demographics and local economic conditions playing secondary roles.
High school accomplishments stand out as the clearest drivers of regional employment. Career and Technical Education (CTE) is especially powerful: concentrators and students who take more CTE courses are consistently more likely to find meaningful regional work, and this advantage endures 10 years after graduation. Academic performance, measured by ACT and MCA scores, also matters. Lower scorers are more likely to transition earlier into the workforce, often finding employment in their home region. Higher scorers, by contrast, tend to pursue postsecondary education and eventually secure meaningful work elsewhere in Minnesota. PSEO participation provides an early push toward persistence and statewide opportunities, but it reduces the likelihood of staying in regional employment over time.
Demographics create important differences in access to regional work. Students in special education are far less likely to achieve meaningful regional employment and are instead overrepresented in non-meaningful work or disconnection. Economic status also plays a role: students from higher-income backgrounds are more likely to move into statewide opportunities, while lower-income peers are somewhat more concentrated in regional jobs, but also at higher risk of disconnection. Gender differences are small but consistent, with men more likely to be in meaningful regional jobs and women more often outside the regional workforce. Race and ethnicity show very modest overall effects; white graduates are slightly more likely to secure regional jobs compared to peers of color.
High school characteristics and local context shape the structure of opportunities available. Rural graduates are more likely to remain in meaningful regional employment, while urban graduates are more likely to move into Minnesota-wide jobs. County-level conditions matter: stronger local economies with lower unemployment and higher wages increase the chances that graduates find meaningful regional employment, while weaker counties increase the likelihood of disconnection. Regional (EDR) differences exist but are comparatively modest.
Taken together, the story is clear: for non-college graduates, CTE engagement is the most reliable path into meaningful employment in the region. Lower academic scorers and rural graduates are also more likely to remain rooted in local work, while higher academic achievers and those with early postsecondary exposure often leave the region for broader Minnesota opportunities. Demographics highlight groups at risk of missing out on regional work, and county conditions reveal where local economies either anchor graduates in meaningful jobs or push them toward disconnection.

Ranked Importance for Regional Employment (Most → Least)

CTE Engagement (Accomplishments: achievement + total courses) – strongest, most consistent predictor of meaningful regional work.
ACT & MCA Scores (Accomplishments) – lower scorers more likely to enter and remain in regional jobs; higher scorers more likely to leave the region.
Special Education Status (Demographic) – persistent disadvantage, much less likely to secure regional work.
Economic Status (Demographic) – lower-income grads somewhat more region-bound but also more disconnected; higher-income grads more mobile across MN.
PSEO Participation (Accomplishment) – reduces likelihood of regional employment over time as participants pursue statewide opportunities.
Rural/Urban (HS Characteristic) – rural grads more likely to stay in regional jobs; urban grads more likely to find work elsewhere in Minnesota.
County Conditions (Unemployment, Wages) – stronger local economies increase chances of regional employment.
Gender (Demographic) – men more likely in regional work; women more often outside.
Region (EDR) (HS Characteristic) – modest variation across Minnesota.
Race/Ethnicity (Demographic) – very small effects on regional employment.

👉 The headline story becomes: Among non-college graduates, the most dependable route into meaningful employment in the region is deep engagement with CTE. Regional jobs are also more common for lower scorers, rural students, and men, while higher scorers, PSEO participants, and higher-income students are more likely to move into statewide opportunities instead. Local economic conditions either anchor graduates in meaningful regional work or push them toward disconnection.

title: Pathways After High School – Southern Minnesota
text:
Prediction - non-college grads
This synthesis compares the three binary outcomes:

A: Regional vs. Statewide Meaningful Employment
B: Regional vs. Not Meaningful, Not Attending PS
C: Regional vs. No MN Employment Record, Not Attending PS

Model Performance Across Outcomes

A (Regional vs. Statewide): Accuracy levels were high (≈67–75%), consistently outperforming baseline. This reflects clearer separations in who stays local versus who is mobile within Minnesota.
B (Regional vs. Not Meaningful/No PS): Accuracy was modest (≈58–62%), slightly above baseline. Distinguishing meaningful local work from marginal attachment is harder, as both groups may share vulnerabilities.
C (Regional vs. No MN Record/No PS): Accuracy was moderate (≈56–62%), again above baseline but with declining lift over time. Predictors are strongest in the short-term, while long-term outcomes are harder to forecast from high school data.

Pattern: CART models are most powerful when contrasting regional stayers vs. statewide movers (A), and least predictive when comparing regional stayers vs. those completely disconnected (C at 10 years).

Key Predictors by Outcome

A (Regional vs. Statewide):
Race/Ethnicity, ACT Composite Score, MCA Reading, Economic Status, PSEO Participation.
Interpretation: Academic readiness and mobility pipelines (ACT, PSEO) drive statewide employment; regional employment is anchored by modest academic readiness and lower-income students.
B (Regional vs. Not Meaningful/No PS):
CTE Achievement, Total CTE Courses Taken, Race/Ethnicity, Special Education Status, ACT Composite Score.
Interpretation: CTE participation is the strongest shield against disconnection, while special education and race stratify risks.
C (Regional vs. No MN Record/No PS):
Total CTE Courses Taken, CTE Achievement, MCA Math/Reading, Race/Ethnicity, Special Education Status.
Interpretation: Depth in CTE is consistently protective; academic readiness matters differently over time (math at 1 year, ACT at 5 years, reading at 10). Racial and disability disparities persist.



Interpretation Over Time

Early (1 Year):

A: Modest ACT readiness and low-income students more likely to work regionally.
B: CTE engagement differentiates regional workers from those disconnected.
C: Math skills and ≥3 CTE courses are anchors; special education students face higher risks.

Mid-Term (5 Years):

A: ACT scores, race/ethnicity, and CTE sustain regional employment vs. statewide mobility.
B: CTE remains protective, but race/ethnicity and ACT readiness gain importance.
C: ACT, CTE, race, and income explain who stays regionally attached vs. who disconnects.

Long-Term (10 Years):

A: Regional employment stabilizes among low-income and modest academic performers; statewide employment aligns with higher scorers.
B: CTE depth still matters, but demographic inequities (race, special education) widen.
C: Reading proficiency and CTE achievement are decisive; racial disparities persist even with strong preparation.




Conclusion
Across all binaries:

CTE depth and achievement are the single most consistent predictors of regional employment — anchoring students early and protecting against both statewide mobility and disconnection.
Academic readiness matters, but the form shifts over time: math early, ACT in mid-term, reading in long-term.
Demographics stratify pathways: race/ethnicity, income, and special education status consistently increase disconnection risks or steer students away from regional employment.
Predictive power is strongest in Outcome A (mobility within MN) and weakest in Outcome C (long-term disconnection), reflecting how labor market forces dilute the predictive role of high school preparation over time.



Policy Implications

For A (Regional vs. Statewide): Retain high scorers and PSEO participants by connecting them to local opportunities, since they are most likely to leave the region.
For B (Regional vs. Not Meaningful/No PS): Expand CTE concentrator/completor opportunities and supports for special education students to prevent early disconnection.
For C (Regional vs. No MN Record/No PS): Ensure all students reach minimum academic thresholds in math and reading while expanding CTE access; supplement with long-term workforce equity initiatives to sustain regional employment.
Overall: The region’s workforce stability depends on expanding CTE depth, addressing academic readiness across subjects, and tackling inequities by race, income, and disability.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: Step 1: Data Preparation and Analytic Population
text:
Step 1: Data Preparation and Analytic Population
1.1 Analytic Population
The analytic population is restricted to individuals who:

Graduated from a high school in Southeast Minnesota,
Did not complete a postsecondary credential (ps.grad = No), and
Have complete workforce participation categorizations (“Sustained WF - Region”, “Sustained WF - MN”, “No MN employment record” or “Non-sustained WF”) for the first five years after graduating high school or first five years after exiting post-secondary (but never completing).

1.2 Annual Workforce Participation Classification
For each individual, annual workforce participation status is identified for: - grad.year.1 - grad.year.2 - grad.year.3 - grad.year.4 - grad.year.5
It’s important to note here that the term “grad.year.x” will be switched to mean years after exiting formal education, not just exiting high school.
Each year is classified into one of the following categories:

Sustained WF participation (Sustained WF - Region or Sustained WF - MN)
Non-sustained WF
No Minnesota employment record.

1.3 Workforce Disconnection Indicators
For each annual observation, a binary disconnection indicator is created:

Disconnected (year-level) = Not meaningful workforce participation or No Minnesota employment record, vs
Not disconnected = Sustained WF - Region or Sustained WF - MN

Using these annual indicators, individuals are grouped based on persistence of disconnection across years 1–5:

Persistently Disconnected: Disconnected in 4 or 5 of the first 5 years
Disconnected (Broad): Disconnected in 3 of the first 5 years
Intermittently Disconnected: Disconnected in 1–2 of the first 5 years
Consistently Attached: Disconnected in 0 of the first 5 years

These categories emphasize sustained labor market attachment or detachment rather than point-in-time outcomes.
1.4 Regional Location of Not Meaningful Employment
For years in which individuals are categorized as not meaningfully attached to the workforce, employment location is further classified as: - Within Southwest Minnesota - Outside Southeast Minnesota (elsewhere in Minnesota) - Both (simultaneous employment inside and outside the region)
This classification allows identification of regional underemployment versus regional disengagement.
1.5 Employment Intensity and Job Holding
For each individual and each year (years 1–5), the following employment intensity measures are constructed: - Number of distinct employers during the year - Indicator for multiple job holding (two or more employers)
These measures are used to distinguish underemployment from precarious or fragmented employment.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Step 2: Descriptive and Summary Statistics
2.1 Distribution of Workforce Disconnection
Summary statistics are produced to describe:

The proportion of non-college graduates in each workforce disconnection category
Differences in persistence and intermittency of disconnection

This establishes the overall scope and severity of workforce disconnection in early adulthood.
2.2 Regional Attachment and Job Structure
Among individuals experiencing workforce disconnection, summary statistics examine:

The location of not meaningful employment (within region, outside region, both)
Average and median number of employers per year
Prevalence of multiple job holding

These summaries clarify whether disconnection reflects local underemployment, out-of-region work, or fragmented employment patterns.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: Step 2: Identify Workforce State for 5 Years After Formal Education
text:
Step 2: Identify Workforce State for 5 Years After Formal Education
Next, we need to pull out all the individuals in which we have five years of workforce categories after they either graduate from high school or the last year in which they exited post-secondary attendance.
After that, we will categorize their workforce participation state into the following;

Sustained WF - Region
Sustained WF - MN
Non-sustained WF
No MN employment record.

I already created the annual workforce participation states for every individuals one year after graduation through 15 years after graduation. I will bring that list in and filter it by our analytic population.

annual.wf.states <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/States/annual-seven-states.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, states) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11", "grad.year.12", "grad.year.13", "grad.year.14", "grad.year.15")) 

no_ps_attendance <- analytic.pop %>%
  filter(attended.ps == "No") %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  left_join(annual.wf.states, by = "PersonID") %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023",
         states != "Attending ps",
         grad.year %in% c("grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5")) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n == 5) %>%
  mutate(states = as_factor(states))

last_ps_attendance <- analytic.pop %>%
  filter(attended.ps == "Yes") %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  left_join(annual.wf.states, by = "PersonID") %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023") %>%
  mutate(numeric.grad.year = str_sub(grad.year, -2, -1),
         numeric.grad.year = str_replace(numeric.grad.year, "\\.", ""),
         numeric.grad.year = as.integer(numeric.grad.year)) %>%
  filter(states == "Attending ps") %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarize(last_ps_year = max(numeric.grad.year, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() 

ps_attendance <- annual.wf.states %>%
  right_join(last_ps_attendance, by = "PersonID") %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023") %>%
  mutate(numeric.grad.year = str_sub(grad.year, -2, -1),
         numeric.grad.year = str_replace(numeric.grad.year, "\\.", ""),
         numeric.grad.year = as.integer(numeric.grad.year),
         final.year = last_ps_year + 5) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  filter(numeric.grad.year <= final.year,
         numeric.grad.year > last_ps_year) %>%
  mutate(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n == 5) %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, states, n)

master.annual.wf.five.year.states <- ps_attendance %>%
  rbind(no_ps_attendance) %>%
  mutate(states = str_replace(states, "Not meaningful, not attending ps", "Non-sustained WF"),
         states = str_replace(states, "No MN emp record, not attending ps", "No MN employment record"),
         states = ifelse(states %in% c("Meaningful emp County", "Meaningful emp EDR", "Meaningful emp region"), "Sustained WF - Region", states),
         states = str_replace(states, "Meaningful emp MN", "Sustained WF - MN"),
         states = fct_relevel(states, "Sustained WF - Region", "Sustained WF - MN", "Non-sustained WF", "No MN employment record")) %>%
  select(-n) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  arrange(grad.year) %>%
  mutate(year.after.exit = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup()

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Step 3: Workforce Disconnection Indicators
Next we add another category to determine the level of disconnection, if any, for each individual. Disconnected is defined as any individual that was categorized as not having meaningful workforce participation or no Minnesota employment record in a given year one through five years after exiting formal education.
The level of disconnection is defined as the following;

Persistently Disconnected: Disconnected in 4 or 5 of the first 5 years
Broadly Disconnected: Disconnected in 3 of the first 5 years
Intermittently Disconnected: Disconnected in 1–2 of the first 5 years
Consistently Attached: Disconnected in 0 of the first 5 years


disconnected.level <- master.annual.wf.five.year.states %>%
  mutate(disconnected = ifelse(states %in% c("Non-sustained WF", "No MN employment record"), "Disconnected", "Attached"),
         disconnected = as.factor(disconnected)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, disconnected) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, disconnected, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  filter(disconnected == "Disconnected") %>%
  mutate(disconnected.cat = ifelse(n == 0, "Consistently attached",
                                   ifelse(n %in% c(1,2), "Intermittently disconnected",
                                          ifelse(n == 3, "Broadly disconnected",
                                                 ifelse(n %in% c(4,5), "Persistently disconnected", "A")))),
         disconnected.cat = fct_relevel(disconnected.cat, "Consistently attached", "Intermittently disconnected", "Broadly disconnected", "Persistently disconnected"))

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: Step 4 & 5: Regional Location of Not Meaningful Employment
text:
Step 4 & 5: Regional Location of Not Meaningful Employment
For years in which individuals are categorized as not meaningfully attached to the workforce, employment location is further classified as: - Within Southeast Minnesota - Outside Southeast Minnesota (elsewhere in Minnesota) - Both (simultaneous employment inside and outside the region)
This classification allows identification of regional underemployment versus regional disengagement.
The population of individuals we need are the following;

Did not graduate college
For each individual categorize whether they had not meaningful workforce participation in the region, not in the region, or both.

We will use the master.annual.wf.five.year.states dataset as the starting point. We will have to have the year they graduated high school so when I match up employment records I’m only using employment records for the first 5 years after exiting formal education.

Now we need to bring in the employment data for Southwest graduates and then filter for PersonID that are in the newly created dataset. The columns we are going to keep from the employment dataset are the following;

PersonID: Identifies the graduate from Southwest Minnesota
TimeID: Last day of fiscal quarter
EmploymentOrganizationID: An internal identification for each employer.
EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked: The total number of hours worked by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeQuarterlyWages: The total wages earned by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeTenure: The total number of quarters a worker has been employed by an organization at a specific location, up to an including the current calendar quarter
CountyName: The name of the county corresponding to the County and MNCounty Codes for this Location.


employment.original <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Employment/Employment-Southern.csv") %>%
  drop_na(PersonID)

emp.year <- employment.original %>%
  filter(!is.na(TimeID)) %>%
  mutate(emp.year = str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4),
         emp.year = as.integer(emp.year),
         quarter = str_sub(TimeID, 5,6),
         quarter = ifelse(quarter == "03", 1,
                          ifelse(quarter == "06", 2,
                                 ifelse(quarter == "09", 3,
                                        ifelse(quarter == "12", 4, 0))))) %>%
  select(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked, EmployeeTenure, CountyName, emp.year, quarter) %>%
  mutate(CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1[,c(1,2,10)], by = c("CountyName" = "Name"))

not.meaningful.pop.emp.year <- analytic.pop.annual.wf.states.hs.grad.year %>%
  filter(states == "Non-sustained WF") %>%
  select(PersonID, emp.year)

not.meaningful.emp.quarter <- not.meaningful.pop.emp.year %>%
  left_join(emp.year, by = c("PersonID", "emp.year")) %>%
  mutate(project.pr = ifelse(is.na(project.pr), "Unclassified", as.character(project.pr)),
         in_region = (project.pr == "Southern"),
         unclassified_region = (project.pr == "Unclassified"),
         out_region = c(!in_region & !unclassified_region)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, emp.year, quarter) %>%
  summarise(n.emp = n(),
         any_in_quarter = any(in_region, na.rm = TRUE),
         any_out_quarter = any(out_region, na.rm = TRUE),
         any_unclassified_quarter = any(unclassified_region, na.rm = TRUE),
         any_mixed_qtr =  (sum(c(any_in_quarter, any_out_quarter, any_unclassified_quarter), na.rm = TRUE) >= 2)) %>%
  ungroup()

not.meaningful.emp.annual <- not.meaningful.emp.quarter %>%
  group_by(PersonID, emp.year) %>%
  summarize(multiple_emp_same_quarter = any(n.emp > 1),
            max_emp_in_qtr = max(n.emp),
            any_in_region = any(any_in_quarter, na.rm = TRUE),
            any_out_region = any(any_out_quarter, na.rm = TRUE),
            any_unclassified_region = any(any_unclassified_quarter, na.rm = TRUE),
            any_mixed_region = any(any_mixed_qtr, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(region_location_year = case_when(any_in_region & !any_out_region & !any_unclassified_region ~ "in_only", !any_in_region & any_out_region & !any_unclassified_region ~ "out_only", !any_in_region & !any_out_region & any_unclassified_region  ~ "unclassified_only", TRUE ~ "mixed" )) %>%
  mutate(
    mixed_type = case_when(
      region_location_year != "mixed" ~ NA_character_,
      any_in_region & any_out_region & !any_unclassified_region ~ "in_out",
      any_in_region & any_unclassified_region & !any_out_region ~ "in_unclassified",
      any_out_region & any_unclassified_region & !any_in_region ~ "out_unclassified",
      any_in_region & any_out_region & any_unclassified_region  ~ "in_out_unclassified"
    ),
    both_structure = case_when(region_location_year != "mixed" ~ NA_character_,
                               any_mixed_region ~ "simultaneous",
                               !any_mixed_region ~ "sequential",
                               TRUE ~ NA_character_)) %>%
  select(-any_in_region, -any_out_region, -any_unclassified_region, - any_mixed_region)

We have created a dataset with 49,848 individuals that do not have meaningful workforce participation for any given year up to 5 years after graduating high school that also provides if they had multiple employers in one quarter, the max number of different employers in one quarter for that employment year, and whether the employer was located in the region, outside the region, unclassified, or a mixture of these categories. Another column further refines the “mixed” category into whether it was sequential - meaning the mix occurred in separate quarters - or simultaneous - meaning there was a mix within the same quarter.
Next, we will piece this back together with the entire analytic population and create a complete annual workforce state for all individuals that did not complete post-secondary and has 5 years of workforce categories after graduating high school.

Master.not.meaningful <- not.meaningful.emp.annual %>%
  left_join(hs.grad.year[,c(1, 8)], by = "PersonID") %>%
  rename(hs.grad.year = grad.year) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = emp.year - hs.grad.year,
         grad.year = paste("grad.year.", grad.year, sep = "")) %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.year) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11", "grad.year.12", "grad.year.13", "grad.year.14", "grad.year.15"))


Master.annual.wf.states.disconnected <- master.annual.wf.five.year.states %>%
  left_join(Master.not.meaningful, by = c("PersonID", "grad.year")) %>%
  unite("wf.states.refined",
        states, region_location_year, mixed_type, both_structure,
        sep = "_",
        na.rm = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(year.after.exit = paste("after.ed.", year.after.exit, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, year.after.exit, wf.states.refined) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year.after.exit, values_from = wf.states.refined) %>%
  left_join(disconnected.level[,c(1,4)], by = "PersonID")

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Distribution of Workforce Disconnection
Summary statistics are produced to describe: - The proportion of non-college graduates in each workforce disconnection category - Differences in persistence and intermittency of disconnection
This establishes the overall scope and severity of workforce disconnection in early adulthood.
Let’s first examine the disconnected categories among these individuals. The level of disconnection is defined as the following;

Persistently Disconnected: Disconnected in 4 or 5 of the first 5 years
Disconnected (Broad): Disconnected in 3 of the first 5 years
Intermittently Disconnected: Disconnected in 1–2 of the first 5 years
Consistently Attached: Disconnected in 0 of the first 5 years

PERSISTENCE OF DISCONNECTION — DISTRIBUTION Non-College Completers, Southeast Minnesota
Among the 32,878 non-college completers with complete five-year workforce participation records, the distribution across disconnection categories is striking and sobering.
Persistently disconnected (disconnected in 4 or 5 of the first 5 years): 15,286 graduates — 46.5% of the analytic population. Nearly half of non-college completers in Southeast Minnesota experience chronic labor market detachment in the first five years after exiting formal education. This is the largest single category by a substantial margin.
Intermittently disconnected (disconnected in 1 or 2 of the first 5 years): 8,407 graduates — 25.6%. This group experiences some disconnection but achieves sustained attachment in most years, suggesting a transitional rather than chronic labor market relationship.
Consistently attached (disconnected in 0 of the first 5 years): 5,326 graduates — 16.2%. Only about one in six non-college completers achieves sustained workforce attachment in every one of the first five years after exiting formal education.
Broadly disconnected (disconnected in exactly 3 of the first 5 years): 3,859 graduates — 11.7%. This intermediate category represents graduates who are more often disconnected than attached but do not reach the persistent threshold.
The most analytically important feature of this distribution is its concentration at the extremes. Nearly half the population is persistently disconnected and only one in six is consistently attached, with the intermediate categories accounting for the remaining 37%. This suggests that early-career labor market attachment is not primarily a transitional challenge that most graduates work through over time — it is a durable structural condition that separates a large and persistent disconnected group from a much smaller consistently attached group. The bivariate analysis identified CTE engagement as the primary predictor of regional employment attachment among non-completers, and the persistence analysis will examine whether CTE engagement similarly differentiates between chronic disconnection and consistent attachment.

data <- master %>%
  group_by(disconnected.cat) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         data_id = seq(n()),
         disconnected.cat = fct_relevel(disconnected.cat, "Consistently attached", "Intermittently disconnected", "Broadly disconnected",  "Persistently disconnected")) %>%
  write_csv(., "Data/Claude/analysis_non_college_deeper/persistence-distribution.csv")

plot <- ggplot(data, aes(disconnected.cat, pct, fill = disconnected.cat)) +
  geom_col_interactive(position = "dodge", aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(disconnected.cat, "\nN: ", comma(n), "\n%: ", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  geom_label(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, color = "black", size = 5, position = position_dodge(width = .9)) +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Percent share of non-college grads,\n2008 - 2018 high school grads")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  theme_bar+
  scale_fill_manual(values = brewer.pal(n = 5, "RdYlBu"),
                    guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = .9))

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Regional Attachment and Job Structure
Among individuals experiencing workforce disconnection, summary statistics examine: - The location of not meaningful employment (within region, outside region, both) - Average and median number of employers per year - Prevalence of multiple job holding
These summaries clarify whether disconnection reflects local underemployment, out-of-region work, or fragmented employment patterns.
Let’s start with the distribution of the various workforce states with the newly defined categories within “Not meaningful” but not all of them because it will get too messy. Let’s first do the following categories;

Attending ps
Meaningful emp region
Meaningful emp MN
Not meaningful

In only
Out only
Unclassified only
Mixed

No MN emp record

DETAILED WORKFORCE PARTICIPATION DISTRIBUTION BY YEAR AFTER EXITING FORMAL EDUCATION — NON-COLLEGE COMPLETERS
The detailed distribution reveals important patterns within the non-sustained workforce participation category that the point-in-time analysis could not capture. Non-sustained employment is disaggregated into four subcategories — within region only, outside region only, unclassified only, and mixed — which clarifies whether non-sustained participation reflects local underemployment or regional disengagement.
SUSTAINED ATTACHMENT
Sustained regional employment grows steadily from Year 1 (24.9%) through Year 5 (30.5%), gaining approximately 5.6 percentage points over the five-year window. Sustained MN employment shows a similar upward trajectory, rising from 9.8% at Year 1 to 15.3% at Year 5. Combined sustained employment — in region or elsewhere in Minnesota — rises from 34.7% at Year 1 to 45.8% at Year 5, a 11.1 percentage point gain that reflects the gradual labor market integration of non-completers over the early career period.
NON-SUSTAINED EMPLOYMENT
Total non-sustained employment declines from 39.3% at Year 1 to 28.3% at Year 5, with the decline concentrated in within-region non-sustained employment (19.9% to 11.1%) and mixed employment (12.4% to 6.4%). The within-region non-sustained category — graduates employed in Southeast Minnesota but below the sustained threshold — is the largest non-sustained subcategory at all five time points and its steady decline from 19.9% to 11.1% is the clearest evidence of labor market integration over the observation window. Some within-region non-sustained graduates are progressing toward sustained regional employment; others are cycling into the no-MN-record category.
Outside-region non-sustained employment (elsewhere in Minnesota but below the sustained threshold) remains remarkably stable at approximately 6.2-6.6% across all five years — showing essentially no trend in either direction. This stability suggests a persistently small population of graduates with fragmented out-of-region employment that neither integrates into sustained MN employment nor disappears from the record.
NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD
The no-MN-record group grows modestly from 25.9% at Year 1 to 30.6% at Year 5 — a 4.7 percentage point increase that reflects graduates cycling out of non-sustained employment and into geographic or informal labor market absence over the early career period. The growth is gradual and consistent year over year rather than concentrated at any single transition point.
The combination of declining non-sustained within-region employment and growing no-MN-record alongside growing sustained employment suggests the population is sorting into two distinct trajectories over Years 1 through 5: a labor market integration trajectory where graduates move from non-sustained to sustained employment, and a labor market departure trajectory where graduates move from non- sustained to no-MN-record. The persistence distribution confirms that the departure trajectory is larger — 46.5% are persistently disconnected compared to 16.2% consistently attached — establishing that among non-college completers, labor market departure is the more common early-career trajectory than labor market integration.

Let’s dive a bit deeper into the disconnected group - not meaningful workforce participation and individuals with No MN employment. The chart below shows the percentage of disconnected individuals (not meaningful, no MN employment record) that fall into each of the refined categories.
DETAILED STRUCTURE OF NON-SUSTAINED AND DISCONNECTED WORKFORCE PARTICIPATION — NON-COLLEGE COMPLETERS
Note: Percentages in this table are calculated as a share of the disconnected population (non-sustained plus no-MN-record) in each year rather than the full analytic population, given the focus on understanding the internal structure of disconnection.
WITHIN-REGION NON-SUSTAINED EMPLOYMENT
Non-sustained WF within region only is the largest non-sustained subcategory at every time point and shows a clear declining trend — from 30.5% of the disconnected population at Year 1 to 20.5% at Year 5. This group is employed in Southeast Minnesota but below the sustained threshold, representing the local underemployment signature identified throughout the bivariate analysis. The steady decline suggests that some within-region non-sustained graduates are transitioning into sustained regional employment over the five-year window, while others are cycling into the no-MN-record category.
OUTSIDE-REGION NON-SUSTAINED EMPLOYMENT
Non-sustained WF outside region only (elsewhere in Minnesota but below sustained threshold) is remarkably stable across all five years — ranging from 10.0% to 11.0% of the disconnected population with no meaningful trend. This stability is analytically interesting — it suggests a persistently small population of graduates with fragmented out-of-region in-state employment that neither integrates into sustained MN employment nor disappears from the record over the five-year observation window.
MIXED EMPLOYMENT PATTERNS
The mixed subcategories — combining within-region, outside-region, and unclassified employment simultaneously or sequentially within a year — collectively account for approximately 18-20% of the disconnected population at Year 1, declining to approximately 11-12% by Year 5. The largest mixed subcategory is simultaneous in-region and out-of-region employment (mixed_in_out_simultaneous), declining from 10.6% at Year 1 to 6.6% at Year 5. This group holds jobs both within and outside Southeast Minnesota in the same year — a pattern consistent with unstable or transitional employment across geographic boundaries. Sequential mixed patterns (working in different locations at different points within the same year) are smaller but similarly declining.
NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD
The no-MN-record share of the disconnected population grows substantially across the five years — from 39.6% at Year 1 to 56.5% at Year 5. By Year 5, more than half of the disconnected population has no Minnesota employment record at all. This growth occurs as non-sustained employment categories decline, suggesting that graduates who do not transition from non-sustained to sustained employment are increasingly likely to exit Minnesota’s formal employment records entirely rather than remain locally underemployed. The trajectory from local underemployment to geographic absence is the dominant pattern of deterioration within the disconnected population over the five-year window.
THE STRUCTURE OF DISCONNECTION
Taken together, these detailed distributions reveal three distinct patterns within the non-college completer disconnected population. The first is a local underemployment pattern — graduates employed within Southeast Minnesota but below the sustained threshold, concentrated in the within-region non-sustained category, and declining over time as some integrate into sustained employment. The second is a geographic fragmentation pattern — graduates with mixed or out-of-region non-sustained employment, stable over time, representing a population with unstable multi-location employment that does not resolve in either direction within the five-year window. The third is a progressive geographic absence pattern — graduates cycling from non-sustained employment of any type into no-MN-record, producing the growing no-MN-record share that dominates the disconnected population by Year 5. The persistence distribution established that 46.5% of non-college completers are persistently disconnected — this detailed distribution clarifies that persistent disconnection increasingly means complete absence from Minnesota’s formal labor market rather than persistent local underemployment.
